S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every battery-related thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, or thermal injury to the relevant regulator within 5 business days of learning of it. A death, life-threatening injury, or fire spreading beyond the battery’s enclosure must be reported within 24 hours.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text:
## Incident reporting
Manufacturers must report every battery-related thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, or thermal injury to the relevant regulator within 5 business days of learning of it. A death, life-threatening injury, or fire spreading beyond the battery’s enclosure must be reported within 24 hours. Manufacturers must provide affected customers with an initial safety notice within 5 business days when an incident indicates a product-specific hazard, and update it promptly as material facts emerge. Reports must include known circumstances, model and serial information, and any immediate risk-reduction instructions. Suspected incidents must be logged and investigated; uncertainty about cause does not delay the initial report.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol before market entry and after a material design or manufacturing change. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% of tested units; a model exceeding 5% may continue to be placed on the market only with regulator approval of a corrective-action plan, and before purchase customers must receive the exact failure rate, sample size, pass/fail status, material safety findings, and risk-reduction information for the model they are considering.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text:
## Thermal testing
Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol before market entry and after a material design or manufacturing change. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% of tested units. A model exceeding 5% may continue to be placed on the market only with regulator approval of a corrective-action plan, enhanced incident monitoring, and clear customer safety information; the manufacturer must retest within 12 months and demonstrate progress toward compliance. Regulators may restrict sales where the evidence indicates an unacceptable risk. Manufacturers must submit exact per-model results, sample sizes, and corrective actions to the relevant regulator. Before purchase, customers must receive the exact failure rate, sample size, pass/fail status, material safety findings, and risk-reduction information for the model they are considering. Public reporting may include aggregated results but not individual-company per-model failure rates.

parameters.quote: Newly installed home battery systems must include a secure remote emergency shut-off capability, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a means for the household to confirm shut-off status. For units already installed when this standard takes effect, manufacturers must offer a compatible retrofit or replacement pathway and complete it within 6 years, prioritizing units subject to an active safety notice or elevated risk.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: Newly installed home battery systems must include a secure remote emergency shut-off capability, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a means for the household to confirm shut-off status. For units already installed when this standard takes effect, manufacturers must offer a compatible retrofit or replacement pathway and complete it within 6 years, prioritizing units subject to an active safety notice or elevated risk.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text:
## Remote emergency shut-off
Newly installed home battery systems must include a secure remote emergency shut-off capability, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a means for the household to confirm shut-off status. Manufacturers must provide clear instructions for customers and emergency responders. For units already installed when this standard takes effect, manufacturers must offer a compatible retrofit or replacement pathway and complete it within 6 years, prioritizing units subject to an active safety notice or elevated risk.

parameters.quote: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text:
## Built-in fire suppression
New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must disclose the suppression system’s capabilities and limitations in customer materials and provide installation and maintenance instructions.

parameters.quote: A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, using validated incident and installed-unit data. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers and relevant regulators when a product-specific hazard is identified, providing practical risk-reduction instructions and updates as material facts emerge.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, using validated incident and installed-unit data. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers and relevant regulators when a product-specific hazard is identified, providing practical risk-reduction instructions and updates as material facts emerge.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text:
## Customer disclosure and recalls
Before purchase, customers must receive clear safety information for the specific model, including its exact thermal-test failure rate and sample size, pass/fail status, material operating limitations, emergency shut-off instructions, and any applicable safety notices. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers and relevant regulators when a product-specific hazard is identified, providing practical risk-reduction instructions and updates as material facts emerge. A manufacturer must initiate a recall when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, using validated incident and installed-unit data. A recall must include direct customer notification, instructions to stop use or reduce risk as appropriate, and a repair, replacement, or refund remedy. A recall requires an effective safety remedy but does not, by itself, require a permanent market ban; regulators retain authority to order additional measures where necessary to protect the public.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Halcyon's flagship 55°C test failure rate is 3.9%, so we can support a 5% maximum with corrective action and retesting for models that exceed it.
ground_truth_claims.message_text: The 7% threshold is above the regulators’ discussed 5% limit. Halcyon’s flagship 55°C test failure rate is 3.9%, so we can support a 5% maximum with corrective action and retesting for models that exceed it. Per-model results must be available to customers considering that model; regulator-only disclosure is not sufficient.

judge_section_notes: The final rules adopt strict incident reporting, a 55 °C / 5% thermal test limit with regulator-approved corrective action and exact customer-facing test rates but no public per-model rates, a 6-year retrofit deadline, built-in suppression at 36 months, and a mandatory 8 per 100,000 recall trigger with prompt customer notices. The deal satisfies both sides' red lines: no public per-model failure rates for Northwind, exact customer test results for Halcyon, a 6-year retrofit window, and a 36-month suppression deadline.
